The contribution of women microenterprises to poverty alleviation in urban Sudan
abstract: In this context, there is a need to assess the effectiveness of microenterprises in improving the socioeconomic conditions of women entrepreneurs and in alleviating poverty.Accordingly, the thrust of the study lies in identifying the effect of women microenterpriseson poverty alleviation in urban Sudan, taking the Khartoum state as a case. The study’s focus is on women with microenterprises or engaged in trading, production, and selling in the informal sector. Hence, the population of the study is the 104 thousand of the self-employed females in KS.350 respondents are selected and random sampling technique is applied considering location of project (market-based, home-based, and street sellers), locality (all KS localities, namely Omdorman, Karrari, Ombada, Khartoum, Jabalawlia, Bahri, Shargalneel) and type of activity (20 different activities are covered). Primary data are collected using a structured questionnaire and individual interviews held with female entrepreneurs in KS as well as by optical observation by visiting the respondents in their locations. Collected data include (1) socioeconomic characteristics including age, marital status, education, family size and housing and place of residence; (2) project related data covering projecttype, activityandlocation; (3) entrepreneurial motivations, opinions, attitudes, perceptions and viewpoints; (4) information on familyincomeand assetsbeforeand after the establishment of the project; (5) sources of funding; (6) marketing, competition and overall performance; and (7) problems and constrains. Secondary data are gathered from various sources including national surveys, censuses and previous studies. Both primary and secondary data are analysed using descriptive statistics and cross tabulation imbedded in the advanced data analysis module of Microsoft Excel. Major findings of the study show that the implemented poverty alleviations plans have contributed to alleviate poverty in the study area, but poverty still widespread. Despite the significant role of the government plans, the average performance remained minor and limited. The study results show that poverty has a woman’s face as there are more women than men who suffer from abject poverty in urban Sudan. It is also revealed that, women’s microenterprises are important elements for an effective poverty reduction strategy, as many respondents confirmed that their business is the only source of family income, which support the assumption that women’ projects is a solution for many families to move out of poverty. This is confirmed as well by the findings that 67% of the women entrepreneurs consumed the income they gained from their projects on daily basic needs, mainly food for the family, especially for women-headed household.Female entrepreneurs' age, marital status and education and family size are all found to be influential factors for their entry into business and in general the culture of self-employment is getting widely accepted with lesser rush to be employed by the public sector. This being reported, female entrepreneurs have also identified several constrains and challenges such as the limited access to finance, difficulties in the marketing of their products, the complex administrative procedures and the government’s fees and taxes.

title: The impact of Fiscal Instruments on Fertility: A Synthesis of the Economic Theory
abstract: IntroductionA general decline in fertility that can be evidenced in developed countries raises the question about the implementation of possible pronatalist government policy. This type of policy can be introduced through fiscal instruments posing incentives to have more children. Naturally, the key issue is to determine whether fiscal policy instruments, such as: income taxes, consumption taxes and subsidies on children may affect fertility in a meaningful way. In general this issue can be considered from both theoretical and empirical point of view.The present work mainly focuses on the first approach, making a synthesis of existing economic theory in terms of the postulated effects of fiscal instruments on the number of children in families. At the same time the details of individual solutions are characterized from a methodological point of view, high- lighting the two prevalent classes of models: the life cycle models with taxpayer having children and multi-period overlapping generation models. Unfortunately some simplifying assumptions of these models undermine the practical utility of a part of the obtained results.A survey of the theory could be useful for stating the new hypotheses for empirical testing, for the development of better economic models and for the determination of the state policy promoting fertility. From the conducted review it can be seen that regardless of the context of redistribution of wealth the fiscal instruments should affect the number of children in households. At the same time there is more than one effective pronatalist policy that can be implemented. In most cases such a policy should also cover more than one fiscal policy instrument stimulating higher fertility.The article is constructed as follows: Firstly, the theoretical literature is reviewed with a critical assessment of its assumptions and outcomes. Secondly, in conclusion, further theory development is provided which can also be treated as postulate for future research.1. The taxation of family when fertility is exogenousThe family size can be driven by economic factors. This statement was firstly proposed by G. Becker, who started the theoretical discussion on the possibility of the social state policy stimulating the optimal number of children. For example, if the choice of consumption and fertility is simultaneous then in the overlapping generation framework with altruistic parents, the fertility should be positively affected by: the world's long-term real interest rate, the degree of altruism and the growth of child-survival probabilities and negatively affected by the rate of technical progress and the growth rate of social security (Becker, Barro, 1988). Therefore the taxation can decrease the fertility rate only in one generation and it does not impact the optimal path of fertility rate if the long term interest rate remains unchanged. There are two caveats to this approach; firstly it is dubious whether altruism is an important factor in fertility decisions; secondly the fertility could be considered exogenous or endogenous. Nevertheless it should be noted that the many theoretical works assume fertility to be exogenous (Mirrlees, 1972; Cremer, Dellis, Pestieau, 2003). It means that the number of children stays beyond the control of families. This assumption is often used as a starting point for comparison with the solutions implied by models of endogenous fertility. However, it seems implausible to set up the total lack of control over the number of children in families*.The optimal linear taxation of family size literature was initiated by the paper of J. Mirrlees (1972). He constructed the economic model with uncertainty, different tastes and unequal exogenous fertility across families. Based on the distributional reasoning, the taxation or subsidization of family size had been proposed. According to his statement, the families with marginal product of labor below the average product should be taxed and families with marginal product exciding the average one - should be subsidized. …

title: Ill health and agricultural production: evidence from Kogi state of Nigeria.
abstract: This study was carried out to analyse the impact of ill health on agricultural outputs in rural areas of Kogi state, central Nigeria. The motivation derives from the fact that rural areas which are strategically important for national food security are more prone to health hazards as a result of the poor nature of health services arising partly from neglect by government. The objectives were to present the socioeconomic characteristics of the rural farm households and identify the prevailing health and agricultural production nexus in the area. The use of multistage random sampling procedure was employed in the selection of 263 rural households for questionnaire administration in order to elicit relevant data related to their farming enterprises and health. The use of descriptive statistics and production function analysis were employed. The study revealed that the average age of the household heads was 46.4 years while the average household size was 6.5 persons. Also, the average farm size was 1.43 ha and the average number of years of formal education was found to be 7.4. Furthermore, the study revealed that the most prominent disease conditions affecting farm families were malaria fever, typhoid fever and diarrhea and these led to an average of 8.2 days reduction in time available for farm work in a farming season. Result from the production function analysis revealed that the elasticities of farm size (0.419), family size (0.099), number of contacts with extension staff (0.018), labour (0.012) and naira amount of credit accessed (0.25) were positively signed and significant at 1%, 10%, 1%, 5% and 1% respectively; while number of days of farm work lost to ill health was negatively signed (- 0.09) and significant at 5%. Findings suggest that focusing on number of days of farming activities lost to ill health in a household might help elicit a clearer picture of the effect of transient ill health on agricultural production. More research and development effort in the provision of and accessibility to health care in the rural areas in order to reduce the incidence of diseases are recommended. Such efforts should also include the provision of adequate health and environmental education for the rural population as the most common ailments discovered in the study area are actually hygiene and environment related.

title: The Other Jack Tanner: Shaw and Robert Loraine
abstract: Robert Loraine, whose biography has preoccupied Lanayre D. Liggera for many years, was born into a theatrical family. Apprenticed to the stage from an early age, he was in London by the 1890s, and, in the early years of the new century, was trying his luck in the United States, hoping to find an avenue to fame and fortune.Loraine knew something of Bernard Shaw, having drawn a favorable mention from the sometime theater critic. Aware that the critic was also a playwright, whose plays had been published if rarely performed, he had arranged to have Shaw's plays sent to him as and when they might appear in print, which is how he came to have a copy of Man and Superman. As he read it, on a train from Boston to New York, he realized that this was the discovery that had hitherto eluded him. “Whether I cried Eureka or no,” he later wrote, “I knew at once this was a marvellous play—simply bound to succeed in the theatre—and danced a jig of delight up and down the corridor of the train, elated beyond bounds by the brilliance of the book itself, and rejoicing at the prospect of producing and acting in a masterpiece.” Loraine's eureka moment came in the nick of time. He had spent two years searching without finding anything that matched his ambition, and he was seriously considering giving up acting altogether.Convinced that he had at last found the vehicle that would make his name, Loraine set about obtaining the American rights to the play. Having secured them (for a down payment of two hundred pounds against 10 percent of the eventual gross receipts), he sought an American manager to back him, but without success. He then arranged to meet Shaw and secure his cooperation, and was able to do this when, back in London, he attended the matinee performance of Man and Superman at the Court Theatre on 6 June 1905. He was promptly invited to lunch the next day at Adelphi Terrace to discuss his plans. And he also found his backer, the producer Charles Frohman, who had seen the play at the Court ahead of Loraine's arrival in London, and was seeking the owner of the American rights.Loraine claims that Shaw gave him carte blanche to produce Man and Superman in New York. In her exhaustive account of Loraine's life, Liggera says that he received a marked up copy of the play from Shaw. This was presumably a duplicate of the Court promptbook, with the changes necessitated to account for the omission of the third act, and also the deletion of the lengthy dialogue in the first between Tanner and Ann concerning “the birth of the moral passion,” as Shaw described it. Loraine, however, had no intention at all of reproducing the Court production, and Channing Pollock writes in a memoir that he spent part of 1905 preparing the script for Loraine's staging of the play. In particular, Loraine saw Tanner quite differently from Granville Barker (and Shaw). Indeed, he was surely obliged to see him differently. At the Court, Granville Barker had been made up with a prominent red beard to look like Shaw himself, and perhaps thereby to give the character a more forceful presence. But this local allusion would not have been recognized by a New York audience. Loraine's Tanner would be impetuous, vigorous, and comic, where Barker's was subtly witty and thoughtful.Shaw gave a summary account of the difference between the two Tanners in one of his contributions to Winifred Loraine's 1938 biography of her erstwhile husband, which has been mined diligently by Liggera. He found Loraine to be “perfection throughout the first half while Tanner is victorious and irresistible. But when Ann's turn came and Tanner went down to defeat and despair at her hands—this part had been performed to Shaw's complete satisfaction by Harley Granville-Barker—Robert simply would not give in.”However, there was much more that differentiated Loraine's production than his approach to Tanner. He conceived the play as a star vehicle with spectacular settings and effects. The first act was reset in an elegant Virginia mansion, with a veranda, rather than in Roebuck Ramsden's Victorian library in London, with its iconic busts. Most spectacularly, the second act was dominated by a flashy motorcar, in which of course Loraine drove off at the end of the act. Liggera has rescued a photograph of what appears to be the last act replete with an elaborate network of paths and steps, affording a variety of vantage points.Loraine's production was a tremendous success, by far the biggest for any Shaw play up to that point and for a long time in the future. Following its New York run, and the American tour that followed, a remarkable sequence of some 250 performances in all, Loraine returned to London to perform Tanner at the Court. This opportunity had arisen because Barker was busy preparing for his future when the Vedrenne-Barker management shut up shop at the Court, in the throes of writing a new play, Waste, and contemplating the possibility of going to New York where a so-called New Theatre was under consideration. Shaw favored this idea: “There is a tide in the affairs of men, as our national bard has well observed,” he told Barker.Liggera calls the Man and Superman revival at the Court—with Loraine, absent the Shavian beard, in place of Barker—a new production. The novelty was Loraine. For the rest, the settings and most of the supporting cast were the established Court production, into which Loraine had to be fitted.Shaw's favorable description of Loraine's Tanner was not of the New York performance of course, which he never saw, but rather what he elicited for the Court revival, and therefore much of Shaw's own making. This is clear from a lengthy letter he sent to Barker, describing how Loraine had been accommodated, or not, at the Court, which, Shaw told Barker, Loraine “loathed.” “Loraine, who always starts a Company by sacking at least three members of it after the first rehearsal to intimidate the rest, is aghast, and has impulses, which recur at intervals of ten minutes, to take the next boat back to America and leave you to play Tanner.” Shaw claimed to have “assimilated all of his business that is to the good” and “utterly rejected the starry part of it.” For example, in act 2, Loraine had wanted to place the car in the middle of the stage, as he had in New York. Setting it like this would enable him “to deliver the great speech about the tyranny of mothers enthroned in the motor car, with Lillah [McCarthy] somewhere under the wheels with her back to the audience.” Shaw continues, “I immediately saw the value of the idea, and put Lillah in the car in a fascinating attitude with her breast on the driving wheel and Loraine ranting about on the gravel…. [H]is dismay imparts an invaluable quality of earnestness to his acting. He feels that he is on the brink of catastrophe, which is exactly what one wants from Tanner.” Shaw was not, however, able to overcome the difficulties posed by Loraine's refusal to give in to McCarthy's Ann, and she was evidently discomfited by his attitude to her. “It is clear to me that he has never had an Ann to give himself in to,” Shaw wrote to Barker. What's more, and perhaps understandably, as Shaw later told Edith Evans, “Lillah hated him.” Shaw, however, looking to the future, extolled Loraine's qualities, telling Barker he was “far and away the best alternative to yourself that we have been able to find,” and so he cultivated his friendship.There remained one important production at the Court before the Vedrenne-Barker management there closed. This was the first performance of the “Don Juan in Hell” scene, given for a handful of matinees, in which Loraine played Juan, a performance that greatly enhanced his reputation. Granville Barker's secretary, Allan Wade, who had been critical of Loraine as Tanner (“his method … seemed to me to consist in charging at the part, head down, as if he were taking part in a rough football game”) made a particularly acute observation about his Juan. The part, as Wade said, calls for “an astonishing feat of memory.” To accomplish it, he revealed, Loraine had rehearsed Juan with the assistant stage manager every day that he had a performance to give. Wade makes the point that this was because he was now playing a “long and difficult part with which he was unfamiliar,” quite the opposite of his Tanner.Man and Superman became Robert Loraine's talisman, and he revived the play several times, both in London and on tour in the United States, as well as once more in New York. He performed Tanner for the last time in 1932.Loraine was cast in other Shavian roles in London in the years leading up to World War I. In Getting Married, he played St. John Hotchkiss. Liggera says, somewhat dismissively, that this was the first time Loraine had portrayed an unpleasant character. Nevertheless, Hotchkiss is “first cousin” to other young Shavian men, like Tanner, Valentine, and Charteris, as Desmond MacCarthy pointed out long ago. “Perhaps I should not have understood, though I should certainly have enjoyed him,” MacCarthy wrote, “if I had not known his relations.” Charteris, in The Philanderer, was a role that attracted Loraine, and one for which Shaw thought him well suited, although, in the end, not one he ever played. He did, however, play Bluntschli in Arms and the Man, and revived it after the war, when it had a markedly different effect on audiences.There were also roles which he might have played but didn't. One such was John Tarleton in Misalliance. Both Liggera and Stanley Weintraub (in his foreword to her book) take note of a balloon excursion undertaken by Shaw, Loraine, Barker, and Shaw's sister-in-law in 1906. “This historic trip would give Shaw the information to write Misalliance,” Liggera writes. This is simply nonsense. Misalliance was not written until 1909, and became Shaw's contribution to the repertory experiment at the Duke of York's Theatre. It drew on a diverse array of sources, but there is no balloon excursion in the play. It is true that there is an aviator, and that, by the time Shaw came to write it, Loraine had developed an avid interest in flying. The second act of Misalliance—not the play itself, as Weintraub mistakenly suggests—begins with the arrival from his crashed plane of Joey Percival, who, like Loraine, is interested in breaking aviation speed and distance records. It is the case that the first name of one of the brothers whose company supplied the balloon for the 1906 excursion was Percival, but this is a tenuous connection at best.In 1909, just as Loraine's interest in taking to the skies was stirring, he played Mitchener in Shaw's one-act suffragette squib Press Cuttings. Since the Lord Chamberlain had refused a license on the grounds that the characters' names, Balsquith as well as Mitchener, were too easily identified with actual politicians and generals, the performance, which was given twice only at the Court, was announced as a “Private Reception,” and there was no charge for admission, a recognized way of evading the censorship.Of the parts Loraine might have played but didn't, the most interesting, surely, is Henry Higgins. In 1913, having given up flying and once more back in America hoping to restore his damaged finances, Loraine told a reporter (a clipping that has apparently eluded Liggera's well-filled net) that Shaw was writing a new play for him. This can only have been Pygmalion, and indeed there is ample evidence that Shaw wanted Loraine for Higgins, another Shavian character trailing aspects of Loraine's own personality. In the event, however, he did not create Higgins because Mrs. Patrick Campbell, who had already had to work with Loraine, told Shaw he must choose between them: he could not have both. Relying on Margot Peters's biography of Campbell, Liggera quotes from letters between Shaw and Mrs. Pat, but both she and Peters miss Shaw's comment to Barker: “she dreads [him] as he dreaded Lillah—ha! ha! Nemesis!”What makes Loraine a particularly interesting biographical subject is that he was not merely an actor. Indeed, when he took up flying he rapidly attained a reputation as a flier to match, and enhance, his stage fame. He expended a quantity of his theatrical earnings on his aeronautical reputation. The same spirit of adventure carried him into the military in both the Boer War and World War I. Liggera's sources enable her to give a fairly full account of his experiences in both conflicts, as well as of his flying career.After World War I, in which Loraine was seriously wounded, he returned to the stage. He had some success at first, perhaps because he was seen as a war hero. He mounted a notable production of Cyrano de Bergerac—an eminent star vehicle that Loraine had had his eye on since before the war. Indeed, it might be said that panache was a defining characteristic of his stage personality. He now surrounded himself with actors who were veterans of the war. He also revived Arms and the Man, which, as he pointed out to a journalist, played rather differently following the slaughter of 1914–18.Despite a severely damaged leg, Loraine continued to appear on stage, and to do so without exhibiting any physical limitation. Shaw went to see him in Cyrano, and noticed that there was no trace of a handicap in his performance. But when he met Loraine afterward, and they walked away from the theater together, the limp was pronounced and Loraine needed a cane. Violet Vanbrugh reports Loraine's response to Shaw's enquiry about this: “The footlights make me another man. I have no disabilities on the stage except any assumed for the character I am playing.”It may have been the fact that Shaw devoted his 1925 Nobel Prize money to a foundation for the translation of Swedish plays into English that drew Loraine's attention to what would be his final major theatrical achievement: Strindberg's The Father. Strindberg's translator and biographer, Michael Meyer, made an acute and penetrating comment about Loraine's effectiveness as the tormented father. It was no coincidence, he wrote in 1975, that Loraine was one of only two actors to have thus far fully succeeded in Strindberg in Britain, and this was because he was an actor “of a most un-English, one might almost say continental vehemence … and consequently … difficult to cast in roles of ordinary human dimensions.”The last decade of Loraine's career was marked by difficulties, personal as well as professional, and his health was vulnerable. He played no new Shaw roles; the only one left to him, after the postwar Bluntschli, was —Tanner. He clung to the hope of a revival of Man and Superman. A plan for him to spearhead a campaign to spread Shaw's fame in Australia lingered but came to nothing. There were discussions of a an American première of the full four-act version of Superman, but they too came to nothing, chiefly, it seems, because the Theatre Guild, which had a virtual monopoly over productions of Shaw's plays in New York, thought Loraine “too old” for Tanner. He was fifty-six when he managed a comeback, starring in Superman for the last time, in Newport, Rhode Island, in the summer of 1932. Notwithstanding the Great Depression, there was still money in Newport. Liggera cites a perceptive review from the Newport Times: “Mr. Loraine's diction is something to be admired…. There are passages in the play which call for long expressions of opinion from the leading character, and he gave them with a skill which only a master has…. He carried the action forward in a manner which kept the audience sharply alert, and the heavy applause which greeted him was truly deserved.”Lanayre Liggera has devoted half a lifetime to Robert Loraine's diverse career. She has drawn on an enormous quantity of information, ranging from actors' autobiographies and university archives to clippings files, correspondence with actors (such as Evans and John Gielgud, who knew Loraine), and numerous conversations with Robert Loraine's daughter Joan, who gave her access to family papers—and she has had the assistance of Dan Laurence and Stanley Weintraub. She seems never to have found a fact that she doesn't want to share with us, and for this alone her book will be appreciated. The story she tells is certainly fascinating. Nevertheless, her irritation with Shaw sometimes shows. Her accounts of Loraine's aviation exploits and of his service in World War I are thorough.Sad to report, the text of this publication is seriously disfigured by a quantity of errors. Arms and the Man was not first produced in 1874 nor The Devil's Disciple in 1879. Jack Tanner's pamphlet is not titled “The Revisionist's Handbook.” The Mecca of English cricket is Lord's cricket ground, not “a lord's cricket ground.” Robert Falcon Scott was not a lord, although he would no doubt have been knighted, as other members of his ill-fated expedition were, had he not perished on the return journey from the South Pole. title: The Determinant of Saving Behavior of Women’s in Urban Ethiopia In Case of Arba Minch Town
abstract: The role of savings in investment and therefore in the development of a country cannot be exaggerated. In poor countries like ours most of the savings is done by households . In this paper the behavior of women saving in Arba Minch town is examined. Total of 50 women’s samples is taken using systematic sampling and Logistic regression model using MLE technique was applied. It has been shown that various factors influence the saving behavior of women’s including credit, employment , income, urban agriculture, family size, education attainment of women’s and age. It is found that, education and age have negative influence on saving but statistically insignificant. Whereas, ownership of urban agriculture and income level have significant and positive effect on saving behavior of women’s. Access to credit and family size has a significant negative influence on the behavior of women saving. Tests of goodness of fit of the model shows the model is fitted, robust hetroscedasticity test prove that the model is free from the problem. The link test also shows the model is correctly specified. Key w ords : Saving, Odds Ratio, Logistic Regression, Marginal Effect, Link test

title: Sharing the Burden or Burden of Sharing? The Role of Sibship in Intra-Family Redistribution and Individual Saving Decisions in Senegal
abstract: Social solidarity, especially within the extended family, play a preponderant role in the context of absent efficient financial markets and low formal public redistribution. These risk-sharing arrangements may however entail some inefficiency costs, through distortions in resource allocation and accumulation decisions. The present paper investigates the influence on savings decisions, of the informal redistribution within the Senegalese extended family. Using a rich nationally representative household survey collected in 2006 in Senegal, I esti-mate the effect of redistributive pressure on saving and transfer decisions. The intensity of the sharing pressure is captured on one hand, by the exogenous size of the sibship and on the other hand, by the position held within sibship as measured by the birth rank and the relative socio-economic situation of the individuals relatively to their fathers. I distinguish between sharable and non-sharable savings, defined as assets that are more or less subject to the family redistribution.
