title: Forward guidance and interest rate pass-through: evidence from New Zealand
abstract: Purpose This paper examines the impact of forward guidance in monetary policy on the pass-through of interest rates in New Zealand by analyzing the degree of both the long-term and short-term pass-through. Design/methodology/approach We use dynamic OLS to estimate the long-term relationship between the official cash rate and the time-deposit rates and various lending rates of New Zealand banks. We use a standard error correction model to estimate the short-term dynamics. Findings The results show that implementing forward guidance improves the degree of long-term pass-through, especially for time-deposit interest rates and longer-term fixed mortgage rates. Furthermore, the markup for various lending rates decreased, and the degree of short-term pass-through increased slightly after the implementation. Practical implications Implementing forward guidance enhances the transmission of monetary policy. Commercial banks are able to respond more quickly to changes in monetary policy by adjusting their deposit and loan rates. Originality/value New Zealand is the first country to mandate inflation targeting. Since its birth in 1990, the 2% inflation target has become the norm for central banks all over the world, including the FED, European Central Bank, Bank of Japan, Bank of England, etc. To our knowledge, ours is the first paper to examine the impact of forward guidance on the interest rate pass-through.

title: The unbearable (financial) burdens of parenting
abstract: Taking Nigel Dodd's work on the social life of money as a springboard (Dodd (2014) 2016), Nina Bandelj makes an impassioned call to extend his approach to studying the social life of money spent on children. In the process she draws attention to the transformation that has taken place in the last few decades in the United States to increasingly view children as sites of parental financial investment. Radically increased spending, saving and borrowing for children is part of relational work, in which today's parents are expected to engage so that they can help their children develop the necessary skills to thrive later in life. A large portion of these parental expenses are educational expenses, like tuition for higher and sometimes secondary education, a wide swath of enrichment activities (like sports and theater camps), and supplementary education offerings like math tutoring and SAT preparatory classes. In her analysis of parental expenses on children, Bandelj also includes expensive mortgages that buy families access to high-performing public school districts. This is because public school education in the United States is mainly financed through local property taxes, and the price of real estate in towns with high-performing schools reflects this. In making her argument, Bandelj echoes Viviana Zelizer's work on the historical and cultural transformation that took place in the United States at the end of the 19th—early 20th century when children went from being perceived as economically useful to being viewed as economically valueless but emotionally priceless (Zelizer, 1985). Recently, Bandelj contends, children are increasingly being treated as sites of parental investment into their human capital. To be sure, Bandelj acknowledges that “the emotional pricelessness of children is still quite salient” (Bandelj, page xx), yet she argues that the “human capital child” is now taking center stage as mere “childrearing expenditures” that characterized parental spending on children in much of the 20th century are replaced with much more ambitious and future-oriented “parental investments”. This means that the social value of children is being transformed yet again. It now encompasses skill-building that can start very early on, as early as in utero, in order to increase children's future productivity and help them command a better price in a future labor market. Moreover, this cultural shift does not only re-evaluate what childrearing should look like today, and what ends it should pursue, but it also puts the spotlight on parental identities and what it means to be a good parent. Citing both qualitative and quantitative data, Bandelj calls for a comprehensive approach to studying how money flows in households, particularly in relations between parents and children. Such a comprehensive approach would not only account for the cultural changes like the widely-shared emphasis on intensive parenting, or the belief in the utmost importance of higher education for children's future life chances. It would also highlight the structural changes that both necessitate greater parental investments, such as growing educational costs, and the simultaneous reduction in public expenditures on education, and facilitate them. To illustrate the latter point, Bandelj presents evidence on the proliferation of various financial tools like the 529 education savings accounts that allow parents targeted and, sometimes, tax-free savings to pay for children's educational expenses, as well as the parental advice industry instructing on the “proper” and “expected” relations between parents and children, including cultural expectations of parental financial obligations toward their children. Finally, Bandelj concedes that the opportunity to invest in children greatly varies by income and race/ethnicity, and depends on the resources available to parents. A lot of what Nina Bandelj states rings true to me. One cannot deny the steep rise of education costs, and the proliferation of various financial instruments to help parents save and pay for these ever-increasing expenses while they also facilitate their children's competing for admission to highly coveted spots in the nation's top colleges. It is a particularly familiar story to anyone who lives in one of the high-cost towns with excellent public schools, or whose children attend highly competitive high schools, whether public or private. In the rest of this essay, I will raise six points that are intended to nuance this picture, and set scope conditions on some of these claims. In a nutshell, parental investment in children's human capital is indeed a compelling story of what parenting is like financially in the 21st century United States. But it is not the only story to be told. My first point is about clarifying or specifying some of the empirical data used (or drawing attention to the data that are absent). Bandelj provides compelling evidence that parental investments in children are riddled with inequality: families with income in the top decile manage to accumulate significantly more financial assets for their children, and white families accumulate more assets than Black and Hispanic families. At the same time, families in the lower income groups as well as Black families with children are more burdened by educational debt—calculated as share of education debt to all assets—than are higher income families and white families. But why are there no data reported for Asian families? It is particularly unfortunate given that educational attainment and college attendance for Asians surpass those of other racial and ethnic groups, and the extremes of intense (aka “tiger”) parenting are often associated with Asian communities. It would therefore be important to include data on parental investments by Asian parents. Other data may have alternative interpretation. We are told that the much higher debt burden that Black families with children carry (Bandelj, xx, Figure 5) suggests they borrow relatively more to pay for their children's educational expenses. But in a recently published report from the Urban Institute that uses a different data source, we learn that while “blacks are most likely to have student loan debt…we do not find evidence that blacks are more likely than whites or Hispanics to borrow for their child's or grandchild's education” (Braga, 2016, emphasis is mine). Two possible explanations are given: one is that Black families are more credit constrained (Bandelj acknowledges this); the other one is that disproportionally more Blacks enroll in college when they are older. In other words, these student loans are likely for their, and not their children's, education. If this is the case, it is a very significant finding but not the evidence to support the argument about parental investments in children. Finally, some of the empirical evidence presented seems very surprising, and warrants more explanation, for example, the reported average size of the education debt held by families with children: it apparently only grew from $948 in 2001 to $4283 in 2016 (Bandelj, p. xx). These numbers seem very low, and likely include families with zero educational debt. It would be important to know the average (or median) debt held by those families with children that have any debt, and the portion of families with children that belong to this category. Is it possible that we are starting to witness a backlash, if not to the social value of higher education, but to its economic value? It could be a result of higher education costs completely divorcing financial reality of even many upper middle-class families, so that it is not uncommon, for instance, for children to matriculate into more affordable but less prestigious colleges than the most select ones that admitted them (many self-styled college advisors, like Harlan Cohen @harlancohen, advocate for prioritizing affordability and graduating debt-free rather than selectivity/prestige when making the final choice of where to attend). According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, only 22% of surveyed U.S. adults believe that “the cost of college is worth it even if someone has to take loans”, while additional 47% say “worth it, but only without taking out loans,” and 29% say “not worth it” (Fry et al., 2024). Granted, the majority believe it is worth it if one does not have to borrow, and the various financial instruments like 529s do help parents save. However, according to the Education Data Initiative, an average American with a 529 plan has $26,783 saved, which is enough only for one year of attending a public 4-year degree college for one child (Hanson, 2024). As much as parents may feel obligated to invest into their children to assure their futures, middle-age parents also feel obligated to help their own elderly parents, particularly if the latter are incurring high medical or long-term care costs (Zaloom, 2019). And the competing needs must put a considerable damper on parental investments in children. Let's look at the numbers. More than 6 million Americans currently use paid long-term services delivered in home and community settings, and more than 2 million people are residents of institutional settings like nursing homes and assisted living facilities, according to the estimates by the Congressional Budget Office. A likely comparable number of people rely on care provided by unpaid caregivers - family, friends, or neighbors - because they struggle to afford to pay for the services: the estimated average annual cost of nursing home care in the United States is $100,000, and an equivalent cost of assisted living facility or in-home care is $60,000 (Hamel & Montero, 2023). And despite what many Americans may think, Medicare—a federal health insurance for the elderly and some younger people with disabilities—does not pay for the type of long-term care that many elderly Americans will require when they are faced with age-related physical or cognitive decline. It only pays for post-acute skilled nursing care of limited duration, usually up to 100 days. Medicaid—a federal and state program providing health coverage for lower income individuals—does pay for long-term care for those deemed eligible. But to become eligible, families need to go through a process called spend-down, which involves demonstrating that they have limited income and no assets (with some exceptions). Currently, Medicaid pays for about half of overall costs of long-term care in the United States. More than 80% of those over 65 who need long-term care services for five years or more will enroll, including, unexpectedly, half of upper-middle-class couples whose lifetime earnings exceed $4.75 million (Johnson et al., 2021). Are we witnessing another possible backlash to the relentless academic pressures on children to develop skills and earn credentials, and to the financial pressures on parents to invest in building their children's human capital? American families are facing a mental health crisis among American children. Arthur Brooks of The Atlantic reports that according to a recent survey, sponsored by the Walton Family Foundation and fielded by Gallup, 38% of respondents between the ages of 12 to 26 have been formally diagnosed with anxiety or depression, including 29% of men and 45% of women. Additionally, half of those that have not been diagnosed report frequent feelings of anxiety, and a quarter of those undiagnosed report feeling depressed (Brooks, 2004; see also Mehasce, Menasce Horowitz & Graf, 2019). A recent book by Jonathan Haidt calls today's teens and young adults “the anxious generation,” and blames the rise in anxiety on the wide availability of smart phones and social media among children starting from very early age (Haidt, 2024). The COVID pandemic and associated lockdowns and broad disruptions to schooling, recreation and social relations further exacerbated this already growing problem (CDC, undated a). And parents are understandably worried. According to the 2022 Pew Research survey, children's mental health struggles were the number one parental concern with 40% of parents stating that they were extremely/very concerned, and another 36% stating they were somewhat concerned (Gramlich, 2023). Academic pressures are likely not the cause of the crisis of mental illness among teens and young adults, but easing academic pressures is often seen as a solution. Many school districts and college admissions have recently introduced more lenient grading and flexible deadlines or made college admissions test-optional.1 In her book Race at the Top: Asian Americans and Whites in Pursuit of the American Dream in Suburban Schools, Natasha Warikoo (2022) explained that school administrators in a North Eastern town she calls Woodcrest, concerned about the effect of academic pressures and competition on student mental health, implemented policies to reduce the amount of homework that teachers could assign. She also notes that this was a move advocated by white parents who were critical of Asian parents' “tiger parenting” style, and threatened by Asian students' higher academic achievements. The issue of mental health brings me to my fifth point. Both in Viviana Zelizer's original formulation of the social value of children, and in Bandelj's current argument about parental spending, there is one particular blind spot: both only consider the value of healthy children.2 In fact, in the “economically valuable” model of the 19th century discussed in Pricing the Priceless Child, only healthy and able-bodied children had any economic value at all. There are many more children today that live with disabilities or serious illnesses than ever before. According to Pew Research, there are 7.3 million students with disability in the United States, and they comprised 15% of students enrolled in public schools nation-wide in the 2021-22 school year (Schaeffer, 2023). Their parents are faced with a very different set of challenges and expectations (Eichenstein, 2015; Kefalas, 2021). Moreover, in a country like the United States, with its relatively low rate of investments in social services to support families with children, such children usually require a lot of necessary but costly medical and nonmedical therapies that need to be paid for out-of-pocket, and many American parents struggle to do so. In 2012, 36% of families with children reported experiencing financial burden because of medical care costs (Cohen & Kirzinger, 2014). This rate is higher than among families of two or more adults without children (25.2%) or among single adults living on their own (20.1%). To think about the specific costs that parents may incur, let's take Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) as an example. Today, one in every 36 children in the United States in diagnosed with ASD (Autism Speak, undated). The costs of raising a child with ASD may include residential care expenses, special education, various medical and non-medical services (such as diagnostic screening, behavioral, physical and speech therapies, etc.) as well as productivity loss for the parents (Buescher et al., 2014). While in countries with socialized healthcare systems much of these costs are borne by healthcare payers, in the United States, a significant portion of these costs are the responsibility of parents and families. All in all, while the financial burdens on parents of disabled children are often a result of very similar processes documented in public education and reported by Nina Bandelj, such as states shifting responsibility for care away from publicly funded programs to families, these families are likely faced with a set of very different challenges from the world of competitive schooling Bandelj describes. My final point is that it is not only the parental investments in child development and education that we should be closely following, but investment in becoming parents to begin with. The American fertility industry is estimated to be worth $8 billion today. The recent WHO report places the rate of infertility at 17.5% globally (WHO, 2023), but many more people outside these statistics rely on assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs), thanks to changes in cultural attitudes and laws that have made parenting by non-traditional parents, such as same-sex couples, single individuals and older people, much more mainstream. In the United States, the cost of the reliance on ARTs varies from a few hundred dollars for a vial of sperm to more than a hundred thousand dollars for a surrogacy arrangement. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2.3% of babies born in the US are born via IVF (CDC, undated b).3 This number also includes babies born to non-American parents, specifically those that travel to the US in search of surrogacy if it is unavailable or restricted in their country of residence. title: How investors account for the quick and the dead
abstract: Poor Ophelia. Gone too soon from the living but now judged harshly for the manner of her departure. What did she do? Was it suicide or an accidental drowning? It mattered for the kind of Christian burial that could be made available to her. (She was, after all, strange, so self-slaughter would come as no surprise.) In Shakespeare's Hamlet, her brother Laertes leaps into her grave, imploring the gravediggers to pile their dirt on both the quick (him, her living brother) and the dead. Of course, it would not be done. These bodies, like so many accounts, were not permitted to mix. In that moment, the social constraints on Laertes and the gravediggers manifested themselves with clarity, revealing “the complex and dynamic configuration of social, economic, and political relations on which [ritual, death, or even] money depends” (Dodd, 2017, p. 244). His choice was not his alone to make (Bandelj, 2012; Zelizer, 1985, 1994, 2012). We are left with the image of an unsalvageable investment now driven, mercilessly, into the ground. Since the publication of Pricing the Priceless Child, sociologists have examined the critical passage from one life stage to another. What is allowed and what cannot be mixed in response to a child's death, Zelizer asked. How does the death of a child differ from that of an adult? How do we express these differences meaningfully through our monies? Unlike Ophelia, the dead in Pricing are not suspected of self-sabotage; they become (almost) incalculable and priceless, requiring amends. In the British Journal of Sociology annual address, Nina Bandelj presents us with a kind of Ophelia, taking her point of departure from the death of childhood and the passage to its afterlife. These investments are part of the social life of childhood, and they involve a proliferation of monies. These monetary investments, Nigel Dodd reminds us, “are shaped by a range of historical, cultural, political, and institutional factors. They are complex and dynamic, variable and contested” (Dodd, 2016, p. 9). Bandelj demonstrates that in the US there has been a sharp increase in “parental investments” in children that differ from prior years in which there were simply “childrearing expenditures.” There are now tax instruments such as 529s and investment accounts large enough to purchase a home that are distinct from the monies set aside of schooling such as books, childcare, clothing, toys, birthday gifts, graduation presents, and the like. Like the shift from the useful to the priceless child, Bandelj marks the move from child-oriented spending for current times to child-based investments in the future. That future indicates the end of childhood and entry into adulthood–a new beginning. The question for parents and those monitoring them is whether the right investments were made to ensure safe passage to the next stage (Wherry, 2016, 2017). I will begin my commentary with the role of relational accounting in decisions to invest in children's education and will turn to how race works in investment choice. To make race active in interaction is to take into account how racialized histories shape investment priorities as well as the very menu of choices most available in and salient to different communities. I will conclude with a theoretical gem that is a bit buried in the discussion, that of economic entanglements. This final insight helps us better understand how different media of exchange affect other media by virtue of their proximity to one another. What is not fully accounted for in Bandelj's address is the fact that parents were not just investing more in children's education (in terms of dollars), but the cost of education has increased by about 400% over the last 30 years. If this were a home purchase, alarm bells would have sounded, and concerns would have been raised about how risky the investment might be. How could the same house go from $100,000 to $5- or $600,000 in price and cost more to finance? Is the interest rate reasonable or usurious? Is the home, or the educational institution, in the “right” neighborhood? The fact that there was not widespread concern or an insistence on the careful evaluation of this market means that individuals were not evaluating the risks of their investment in the same way as they could have. What were they doing instead? Sensitivity to the price of educational investments has declined as the life-stage significance of the investment has increased (Hayes & O’Brien, 2021; Wherry, 2016, 2017). The normal life-stages include birth, early childhood, the transition into young adulthood, and death. College represents the break between a non-adult and a young adult whose financial obligations are still associated with their families. Whereas parents feel obligated to pay for college expenses, including living expenses, they may not feel obligated to pay for a young adult who is not going to college, except in the case of emergencies. This happens, in part, due to shared expectations about the opportunities that a child should have in the transition to adulthood. Bandelj, Wherry, and Zelizer (2017, p. 7) observe that people are more reluctant to spend money saved for a child’s education because ‘these funds represent and reinforce meaningful family ties– the earmarking is relational’ (see also Zaloom, 2019) … investment monies by definition are uniquely oriented to the future… Wherry (2016, 134–135) advances a theory of relational accounting that accommodates the microlevel relational work involved both with specific earmarks and with collectively held codes that correspond to ritually marked moments or rites of passage. Financial goals such as retirement and college savings are thus morally fixed and structured. Graduations are costly, for example, and the expenses associated with the ceremony are not necessary for the acquisition of the credential or the human capital the graduating student now carries. Family members and neighbors, however, would object to a parent not supporting their child's participation in graduation and might themselves step in to help ensure that child experiences this meaningful right of passage. What is true for graduation is true for other investments in childhood. In a 3 year, longitudinal study of unconditional cash transfers, researchers found that “investments in child-specific goods [books, toys, and programs] and time spent with the child [reading to the child] …increased.” These findings contradict the notion that money is fungible, that these dollars are being used as any dollars coming into the family's coffers would be. Furthermore, their research design allows them to account for “the structure, format or related implementation features” of the cash transfer program. They write, “Notably, these investments occurred during the economically important first few years of children's development” (Gennetian et al., 2024, pp. 7–8). Yet, what they describe as a psychological, non-financial phenomenon, economic sociologists understand as relational accounting (Wherry, 2016, 2017). Relational accounting does not occur in a historical vacuum. How racial identities have formed in a country and how they have been shaped by public policy and by private market privations affect how families interpret and respond to investment opportunities. The racialized history of the United States has transformed some educational opportunities into debt traps. Six years after starting college, for example, a majority of Black students have not graduated but still carry student debts (Addo et al., 2016; Dwyer et al., 2012). With the educational investments being so risky for Black families, why do they pursue those high-risk investments, anyway? For too long, analysts pointed to information asymmetries and a problem with borrowers simply not understanding the stakes, along with students not “knowing the ropes” (how to navigate the college experience successfully). Bandelj turns the spotlight away from information gaps to the very relationships driving and sustaining those investment decisions. Tressie McMillan Cottom (2017) brings our racialized history back into our understanding of debt as it is expressed in the social gospel of education. Investing in one's education is participating in racial uplift. She studies for-profit colleges that train hairdressers, NASCAR technicians, medical and legal office administrators, and nurses along with nurses' aides. These are not the 4-year college experiences that come to mind in so many debates about what college is and who should go. And these college attendees believe strongly that they are investing in themselves. Their college debts, therefore, are positively associated, at least in the early years of having it, with their sense of mastery and self-esteem (Dwyer et al., 2011). There is a social gospel of progress that centers higher education as one of the rites of passage into adulthood (Wherry, 2016, 2017), and compliance to the gospel is socially enforced. While Bandelj's address emphasizes the vast differences in wealth by race that are driving how debts are accumulated for higher education, she does not detail how these material conditions are mobilized through relational work. She uses illustrative interview data from an upper middle-class white father of three to indicate the strong belief in investing in one's children, where “a loan is not the worst thing in the world,” and where it is “heartbreaking” to “want something for your kids that you cannot afford to get.” One has to wonder what the class and race differences are. Would a Black father say the same with a similar level of intensity? And what would happen if, by their actions, they violated their commitment to doing whatever possible to invest in their child's future? Would in-laws, siblings, grandparents, and other community members have a way of sanctioning those actions? How might racialized understandings modify risk tolerance and what effect might they have on investment portfolios? To treat “race as a structure as well as a structuring conditions” as scholars like Bonilla-Silva (2019), Feagin (2013), and Rucks-Ahidiana (2022) have done, is to make dynamic and processual its workings. In this process, the perceptions about and the salience of risk will vary, and that variation will be accomplished through interactional work (Wherry, 2012). Commercial engagements are performances, requiring the partial suspension of disbelief so that risks can be endured and the reactions of others interpreted. If we treat race as a structuring condition of performances, we must ask what individuals “see” right away versus how they exercise strategic ignorance towards facts whose acknowledgment would derail the performance. In other words, when negotiating which media of exchange are appropriate and which ones too risky to put into play, we are also responding to our histories of race and racialization that make some facts more salient than others. These histories of racialization shape how students invest in themselves and how their loved ones also contribute to those investments. Those histories also shape patterns of disinvestment, whereby opportunities that appeared to be capital appreciating turned into asset stripping traps (Wherry & Chakrabarti, 2022). More attention to how investments get racialized would result in an analysis of predatory inclusion (Taylor, 2019) in the higher education marketplace. Whether predatory or generative, monies for education are entangled. By their nature, monies wrap around one another the way tendrils do up the stalks of garden vegetables. Monies reach into the earth and become tied into other root systems. Pulling out a single strand is difficult without harming the very thing that the extrication might protect. How do our monied gardens grow, and under what conditions will they grow to seed? Bandelj begins to address this question with fresh theorizing about what economic entanglement means. She takes inspiration from quantum physics where quantum entanglement means that “aspects of one particle of an entangled pair depend on aspects of the other particle.” Bandelj clarifies further that “entanglement ‘exposes economic actors as practical negotiators employing procedural varieties of action, including commitment, muddling through, and improvisation’” (Bandelj, 2020, p. 255). I would suggest that the concept of entanglements does much more than expose the engagements of practical negotiators; it emplots them—placing monies and their users within a story-line that is being enacted (Alexander, 2004, 2011). To emplot actors engaged in relational work is also to consider the preferred versus the forbidden placements of the media they carry (Alexander, 2004). The exchange media themselves affect one another by virtue of their proximity to one another, their symbolic alignments or their binary oppositions. Some media, by nature or by law, might be repellant in proximity; others neutral or attractive, even before the users of the media take any actions to acknowledge, amplify, repair, cool, or cut a social tie. This means that relational packages are not just toolkits from which actors grab media of exchange (Swidler, 1986); the packages themselves do work once assembled and depending on the historical and the racialized contexts, some packages will resist the inclusion of particular forms of media, or of particular types of participants. The practice of emplotment puts monies into an ongoing narrative—be they assets or liabilities— in ways that prevent ontological rigidities (Somers, 1994). The assets and their ability to act, the liabilities and their power to impose penalties on other assets by way of levies, liens, garnishments, or even shame— they implicate the story of money for children with other stories about the kinds of futures these children deserve. Emplotted entanglements, I argue, might help us understand our “strange investments” in children's education (Dodd, 2011). In the investments parents make for their children, they are cultivating a kind of garden. Some gardens appear deserving of attention and applause, but others appear neglected and deserving only of what they got—the weeds. When too many weeds are permitted to possess the garden, they choke the good growth, leaving more space for the flourishing of bad investments. In time, these weeds can pull down the stronger, more mature trees rimming the original plot. The metaphor of the garden offers a warning even to those in class positions that seem to benefit from the current state of affairs. The conditions of one side can pollute the other. The separation between those in predatory versus non-predatory financial instruments can erode, even if those on the edges of predation do not believe themselves to be in imminent danger. In Bandelj's analysis of the plot, she witnesses childhood investments that have sprouted invasively across a field. There are not just a few but many ways to save and invest; not just a few, but many ways to borrow. As the plot grows wild, she captures the changing value of children and the changing investments made on their behalf. If we learn the lessons Bandelj is trying to teach us, we will revisit our investments, not just those made for children, and we will emplot them in the relational and racialized dramas shaping their salience. None. Data sharing is not applicable to this article as no new data were created or analyzed in this study.

title: Enhancing Rural Credit Accessibility: Key Determinants Affecting Farming Households in the North-West Region of Cameroon
venue: Asia-pacific Journal of Convergent Research Interchange
abstract: The agricultural sector is critical to production and employment in Cameroon's national economy.However, small-scale farmers, who comprise most of the agricultural labor force, often face serious challenges accessing the credit essential to improving productivity and overall livelihood.These challenges arise from lengthy credit access procedures and the lack of collateral among farmers, such as obtaining credit, the required time lag, and the type of collateral securities required.In consideration of these issues, this research formulated policy recommendations for enhancing the availability of agricultural credit by identifying the major determinants affecting such access among small-scale farmers.Data were collected from 247 rural households in the North-West Region of Cameroon through face-to-face interviews.The survey revealed that 76.92% of the households had access to credit, whereas 23.08% did not.A probit regression model was employed to identify the core determinants of credit accessibility.The results indicated that the model was statistically significant and fit the dataset better than a model without predictors, as evidenced by a Wald chi-squared value of 32.22(p-val<0.000).Educational level, land ownership, marital status, occupation, household size, and income earners positively influenced credit access, but the number of children in school had a negative effect.This study uniquely contributes to the literature by encompassing diverse agricultural households rather than cropspecific cases, providing comprehensive insights that can guide policy interventions.Recommendations include reforming land ownership policies, subsidizing educational expenses, and simplifying credit application processes to bolster financial inclusion and rural development.

title: Money, child quantity-quality tradeoff, growth and welfare in a Schumpeterian model with status-seeking in human capital
River Waste to Goldmine: A Tale of Floating Agriculture in Vulnerable Southern Regions of Bangladesh
abstract: ABSTRACT Floating agriculture transforms marshy lands into productive resources, enhancing food security and rural incomes in climate‐vulnerable areas. While prior research highlights its potential as a climate‐resilient practice, gaps remain in understanding the determinants of adoption and long‐term livelihood impacts. Our study addresses these gaps by examining farming procedures, profitability, impacts, and the key drivers and challenges influencing floating agriculture adoption in southern Bangladesh. Data was collected from 158 farmers using a pre‐tested questionnaire between October 2018 and April 2019. Profit function and logit regression models were applied to analyze profitability and socio‐economic determinants, complemented by qualitative methods and causal loop diagrams to assess impacts. Findings reveal that farmers employ both intercropping and monocropping, with a preference for seedling raising (156.37 USD/100 m2) over vegetable cultivation (121.56 USD/100 m2) due to higher profitability. Despite its labor‐intensive nature (73% labor costs for seedling rising vs. 85% for vegetable cultivation), floating agriculture boosts household income, meets local vegetable demand, and reduces reliance on external markets during shocks. Additionally, it provides ecological benefits such as waterweed management and reduced environmental pollution. Floating agriculture also alleviates poverty by enhancing agricultural production and generating a positive feedback loop of increased income, food availability, and improved nutrition and health. Adoption is influenced by age, experience, family size, income diversity, credit access, extension services, and market proximity. However, high capital costs, limited credit, market volatility, and biotic/abiotic stresses pose challenges. To scale up floating agriculture, policy measures should focus on financial support, technical training, cost‐effective innovations, and fostering cooperative farming. Institutional backing is crucial for promoting this sustainable cleaner production practice in flood‐prone regions of Bangladesh and similar global contexts.

title: The relationship between financial literacy and financial performance of registered small enterprises
venue: International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy (2687-2293)
abstract: This study sought to examine the correlation between the financial literacy of small business proprietors and the performance of their enterprises in the northern region of Tshwane Ga-Rankuwa. The research utilised a quantitative methodology, employing a standardised questionnaire distributed to small business owners. A quantitative methodology underpinned the study's aims in examining a potential association between financial literacy and business performance. Data were examined via STATA/small enterprise, version 17. Descriptive and inferential statistics were conducted to analyse the distribution of study participants and their financial literacy. Multiple linear regression evaluated the relationships between predictor factors (socio-demographic characteristics and financial literacy) and return on assets. The small firms reported low to moderate profits and elevated returns on assets (ROA). Substantial correlations are present among family size, income level, and ROA, contesting the assumptions that education and experience are predictors of performance. Financial performance exhibits good connections with financial literacy and access to financing; nevertheless, the minor associations with knowledge and attitude highlight crucial dimensions of performance. Small firms must to seek methods to enhance profitability and invest in financial literacy. Authorities ought to enhance access to funding for small firms and should evaluate the relevance and quality of education concerning its contribution to financial literacy. The research demonstrated the significant influence of financial literacy and access on forecasting financial performance. Nonetheless, the correlation between financial literacy, attitudes, and actual financial results was less pronounced than anticipated.

title: Legal solutions for fostering sound local finances
abstract: The aging of low birth rates, the movement of the population to the metropolitan area and large cities, and the lack of jobs are causing problems along with the reduction of the local population. Local governments' financial independence and social overhead capital are decreasing, while social welfare expenses are continuously increasing. Local governments with guaranteed autonomy under the constitution shall secure independent resources to sustainably carry out the welfare of local residents and respond to the administrative demands of residents, secure the safety and efficiency of local finances, and ensure autonomy and accountability in financial management. If the fiscal soundness of local governments is not secured, various legal problems arise, such as fiscal expansion, debt growth, inflation, and local financial collapse. In particular, due to the structural contradiction of local taxes concentrated on property tax and acquisition tax due to the recent low economic growth of our country, the slump in the real estate market, the deepening of inflation, and the trend of high interest rates, it is urgent to secure the soundness of local finances due to the decrease in local tax revenues, increase in debt due to the issuance of local bonds, decrease in profits from investment projects, and deterioration of financial structure. It is necessary to devise a direction for the operation and development of local finances that enhances the efficiency of local finances. After discussing the operating system for securing fiscal soundness under the Local Autonomy Act and the Local Finance Act, we present a healthy local financial promotion plan by reviewing legal issues such as rationalization of expenditure management for sound local financial promotion, enactment of the Local Financial Integration Act, revitalization of local financial consolidation ordinances, securing sustainability of local finances, and strengthening external audit systems.

title: Interest Rates and Monetary Policy Implications in an Ageing Economy
The Pivotal Role of Start-Up Ecosystems in Creating a Level Playing Field for Indian Women
abstract: In India, women's entrepreneurship has grown significantly during the past few years. It is both driven by better access to education and by government initiatives and the Women Entrepreneurship Platform, driven by changing societal attitudes toward women entrepreneurship. Women entrepreneurs have made remarkable strides across various sectors from the technology and healthcare sectors to agriculture and manufacturing, thereby leading directly toward the advancement of economic growth, innovation, and financial inclusion. Notwithstanding, these challenges persist to date, which include limited access to capital, societal pressures, and lack of mentorship. According to forecasts, women are estimated to make more contributions in the workforce in the near future. It is here that growth start-ups are expected to bring about a change. The growth of women entrepreneurship in India has given birth to a variety of initiatives by the government towards the same for starters in gender diversity, marking the hallmarks of an inclusive, innovative future for women in business.

title: “Explaining Variation in Child Penalties: The Role of Gender Norms and Policies”
abstract: This paper contributes to understanding global variation in child and marriage penalties by focusing on the role of patriarchal control, gender norms, and public policies. We introduce a new measure of gender norms, the Control Index, which captures women’s ‘freedom to choose’ in key areas of daily life, including mobility, marital choices, workplace rights, and financial independence. Using data from nearly 60 countries, we investigate the extent to which patriarchal control influences the child and marriage penalties, trying to disentangle the still unexplained part of the gender gap. Our findings reveal that higher levels of patriarchal control are strongly associated with larger marriage penalties. In particular, control over marriage decisions is closely correlated with both higher child and marriage penalties, while restrictions on women’s financial autonomy contributes mainly to explaining marriage penalties. This suggests that, in addition to childcare-support policies, financial inclusion for women, could mitigate the effects of patriarchal control and conservative gender norms. Our analysis underscores the importance of addressing these norms alongside public policy interventions to reduce gender disparities in the labour market. JEL Classification Code: J13-fertility, family planning, childcare, children, youth; J16-economics of gender, non-labor discrimination; J22-time allocation and labor supply

title: Determinants of Household Debt: A Systematic Review of the Literature
abstract: Household debt plays a crucial role in influencing the performance of the economy and its vulnerability to shocks. This study synthesises studies on this topic. We used the systematic literature review technique to analyse 97 studies from the EBSCO, Google Scholars, Sabinet African Journals, SAGE, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Springer Link, Taylor and Francis, and Web of Science databases from 2004 to 2024. The results reveal that country-level and household-specific factors are important in explaining debt. We delineate supply-side and demand factors that drive debt. Country-level factors that explain indebtedness include housing prices, unemployment, economic growth, interest rates, inflation, and income levels. At the household level, factors such as education level, behaviour, social status, employment, house prices, income, family size, occupation, wealth, and marital status explain indebtedness. Policies impact loan types differently; therefore, due consideration should be taken and prescriptions should aim to address both supply and demand factors. Future studies should rely on AI-driven methods and techniques that utilise natural language processing capabilities such as sentiment analysis in order to handle large data sets and ensure objectivity.

title: Food and nutrition security of smallholder farmers in Eastern Ethiopia: A comparative analysis of shifters and non-shifters from coffee to khat
venue: Journal of Agriculture and Food Research
abstract: Notwithstanding the substantial progress achieved under the sustainable development goals of 2030 aimed at “zero hunger and malnutrition”, worldwide malnutrition and food insecurity are escalating. This study identifies factors linked to food and nutrition security among farm households in eastern Ethiopia that shifted from coffee to khat and those that did not. Primary data were collected from 788 randomly selected households across the four districts. The calorie intake and dietary diversity score were used to encapsulate food and nutrition security. Descriptive statistics revealed that 74.1 % of households consumed calories below 2550 kcal/AE/day, with an average dietary diversity score of 4.46. Food insecurity rates were 80.2 % for shifting households and 63.4 % for non-shifting households. Similarly, 35.4 % of households had low, 52.4 % had medium, and 12.2 % had high nutrition. Among shifting households, 37.3 % were low, 54 % medium, and 8.7 % high; whereas non-shifting households had 32 % low, 49.7 % medium, and 18.3 % high nutrition security. The probit model showed that food security was significantly associated with age, farmland, cooperative-membership, off/non-farm activities, credit access, market information, and the shift to khat. The ordered probit model indicated that nutrition security significantly influenced by family size, shift to khat, off/non-farm activities, credit access, on-farm income, clean water, and road distance. The findings suggest that policymakers and development partners aiming to reduce food and nutrition insecurity in the study area should focus on the identified variables. • Many households fall below the recommended caloric intake threshold. • Higher food insecurity rates observed in households shifting to khat. • Dietary diversity scores indicate limited variety in household diets. • Key factors for food security include age, land, shift to khat, credit, off/non-farm, market information, and cooperative. • Nutrition security influenced by family size, on-farm income, shift to khat, credit, off/non-farm, distance to road, and water access.

title: South Korea in 2024
abstract: In South Korea, 2024 concluded with unprecedented political turmoil when President Yoon Suk-yeol declared martial law on December 3rd, which was then lifted within six hours. Earlier in the year, the opposition Democratic Party solidified its legislative dominance after a landslide victory in the 22nd National Assembly election, further constraining Yoon’s administration, which was already weakened by scandals involving first lady Kim Keon-hee. On the international front, the re-election of US President Donald Trump ushered in a more transactional approach to alliances, complicating South Korea’s response to North Korea’s escalating militarization. Domestically, rising interest rates, a stagnant housing market, and record-low birth rates fueled debates over urgent reforms. Amid these challenges, South Korea achieved significant cultural milestones, including Han Kang’s Nobel Prize in Literature and the global success of Rosé’s hit song “Apt.,” reaffirming the nation’s growing cultural influence on the global stage.

title: Efficiency of Marketing Channels and Factors Influencing Marketing Channel Choice of Horticultural Farmers: Evidence from Assam, India
venue: Journal of International Food & Agribusiness Marketing
abstract: Marketing of agricultural commodities is challenging due to its high perishability, making the selection of an efficient channel essential for enhancing farm profitability and income. The study examined the efficiency of marketing channels for horticulture crops and factors determining farmers’ selection of channels. It was found that direct marketing is the most efficient channel but least preferred by farmers. Multinomial logit model revealed that factors like access to smartphone and bike positively influenced direct marketing choice, while education, farm size, family size, access to credit, market yard limitations, and preference for bulk selling negatively impacted it. These suggest that policies for promoting the use of mobile technology for marketing and farming, developing user-friendly apps or websites for marketing farm products, introducing farmers-friendly credit systems, and improving rural infrastructure such as cold storage and market facilities, road and transport facilities, etc., should be implemented expeditiously to increase farmers’ direct market participation.

title: Determinants of adoption of home garden agroforestry practice and its role to food security in Southern Ethiopia
venue: International Journal of Agricultural and Life sciences
abstract: Ethiopia's adoption of home garden agroforestry practice is influenced by a number of factors. This study explores the complex network of variables that affect food production, livelihoods, and farmers' decisions to participate in agroforestry in home gardens in the Aleta Chuko Woreda. One common tactic to address food-related challenges is agroforestry. This research aims to evaluate the factors that lead to the adoption of agroforestry practices in home gardens and their impact on food security within the area. The sample households were chosen through a multistage sampling technique. 312 households also took part in the home survey. To triangulate survey data, key informant interviews and focus groups were held. Binary Logit regression models and descriptive statistics were applied. The outcomes of the findings demonstrated the significance of home garden agroforestry practices in the investigated area. Addressing nutritional concerns, and giving households extra revenue streams particularly for women counterparts were all favorable effects. This is due to they have unique knowledge for identification of local crop species. The majority of the area's forest trees are important for preventing and responding to potential climate change extremes and provision of medicinal value. Moreover, homes within the research region stated that technology is crucial for adjusting to and reducing the dangers associated with climate change. The practice of agroforestry home gardens in Southern Ethiopia has a long history. It has a substantial use in the southern Ethiopia adaptation and mitigation to climate change hazards. When it comes to implementing home garden agroforestry, family size, cooperative group participation, educational status, and access to credit and extension services all show statistically significant connections. Thus, in order to help farmers improve their standard of living and improving food security status, the government and other supporting organizations should support home garden agroforestry practices.

title: Public Coverage of Postpartum Services for Immigrants
abstract: Importance: Although 23% of births in the US are to non-US-born birthing parents and 6% of births are to undocumented immigrants, many immigrants have limited access to insurance coverage for postpartum care or contraception, which contributes to substantial health disparities. Understanding policy variation in postpartum coverage for immigrants may lay the groundwork for assessing the association of different policy options with maternal and child health. Objective: To determine if and how each state provides publicly funded insurance coverage during the postpartum period for immigrant birthing parents. Design, Setting, and Participants: Policy documentation from every US state and Washington, DC, was reviewed, and legal epidemiology policy mapping via a qualitative content analysis of policy documentation was conducted. Data were collected and analyzed on an ongoing basis between June 2021 and February 2024. Main Outcomes and Measures: For each state, the postpartum funding mechanism for undocumented immigrants and lawful permanent residents were identified, as well as eligibility criteria, services covered, and the duration of eligibility. Results: A total of 19 states cover some postpartum care with the Children Health Insurance Program (CHIP) from conception to end of pregnancy option, 30 states use Medicaid or CHIP through the CHIP Reauthorization Act Section 214, and 7 states use state-only funds. There was wide variation within each of these mechanisms regarding financial eligibility, services covered, and duration of coverage. Conclusions and Relevance: The results of this qualitative study suggest that there is substantial variation between states in whether and how immigrants can access publicly funded health insurance during the postpartum period. Further research is needed to examine the association between state policies and postpartum maternal health outcomes.

title: Retirement, Social Security Deferral, and Life Annuity Demand
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper contributes to our understanding of wealth decumulation behavior by examining trends in retirement, Social Security claiming, and annuitization decisions. Prior research suggests that while these decisions have high stakes for retirement security, people may not make them optimally. I use data from the Health and Retirement Study to examine the joint timing of these decisions. I show that younger birth cohorts are less likely than older ones to use “parallel” strategies—simultaneously retiring and commencing Social Security, or simultaneously commencing Social Security and a life annuity. Regression analysis suggests that parallel strategies are associated with defined benefit pension coverage and eligibility, being subject to the Social Security earnings test (which forces affected individuals who work while receiving Social Security to delay a portion of their benefits), and poor health. I also find that younger cohorts are more likely than older ones to forgo annuitization altogether—a trend that likely reflects declining coverage by defined benefit pensions, which typically feature annuitization as the default option. Higher real interest rates are associated with both earlier retirement and an increased propensity to start receiving a life annuity.

title: Empirical study on perception of crop insurance scheme among the farmer’s children pursuing agricultural degree in Karnataka
venue: International Journal of Agriculture Extension and Social Development
abstract: Risks associated with farming include those related to weather, productivity, prices, government regulations, international markets, and other variables that affect farmers' earnings. In order to shield farms from production risk resulting from landslides, storms, frost, floods, cyclones, and droughts, the government has implemented crop insurance. However, crop insurance's effectiveness and acceptance are lacking. Therefore, it's important to comprehend how to enhance crop insurance's performance. Farmers have not been very active in purchasing insurance premiums, so it is necessary to look into the barriers to participating in the programme. The particular goals were to assess the barriers to obtaining insurance for crops in the research area and to characterise the socioeconomic characteristics of farmers. With the aid of a carefully designed questionnaire, primary data were gathered from 126 respondents who are the offspring of farmers pursuing degrees in agriculture from several agricultural universities in Karnataka. In order to determine the association between the respondents' level of awareness of insurance for crop shames and their involvement in farming activities, data were evaluated using a correlation statistical method. The study also aims to assess how respondents' awareness of crop protection is influenced by their family size, or more specifically, their family constitution (nuclear or joint family). The respondents had medium level of knowledge about Crop protection (69 (or nearly 55%) said they had no knowledge of crop insurance. Additionally, it is discovered that there is no discernible variation in the respondents' assessments of their level of crop insurance awareness among those with varying family constitutions. There is no discernible difference in the understanding and comprehension of crop protection schemes between respondents from joint families and nuclear families. According to the study, in order to encourage respondents to adopt a few villages while pursuing a degree in awareness-building as part of the curriculum, it is necessary to raise an elevated level of awareness about insurance for crops schemes by means of the course material in the first the semester of their admission.

title: Adjustments to Reduced Cash Transfers: Religious Safety Nets and ChildrenS Long-Term Outcomes
Innovation Potential, Firm Life Cycle, and Cross-Country Productivity Differences
Socio-economic characteristics with knowledge and attitude of perceived by respondents of women regarding women empowerment schemes in Bikaner district of Rajasthan
venue: International Journal of Agriculture and Food Science
abstract: Context: Women empowerment refers to increasing the spiritual, political, social, educational, gender or economic strength of individuals and communities of women. Policies on Women empowerment exist at the national, state and local (Panchayat) levels in many sectors, including health, education, economic opportunities, and gender based violence and political participation. Hence the Government of India launched many schemes especially for women and the constraints faced by them in gaining the benefits of the selected schemes Objective: To find out the relationship of socio-economic characteristics with knowledge and attitude of respondents regarding women empowerment schemes. Methods: The study was conducted in both rural and urban area. For rural area out of nine Panchayat samiti Bikaner Panchayat samiti was selected, from Bikaner one gram Panchayat namely Husangsar was selected and two villages namely Husangsar and Nagasar were selected. For urban area out of two zones i.e. (east and west) two wards namely ward no. 58 (east zone) and ward no. 39 (west zone). Thirty respondents were selected from each village and each ward thus selecting 120 respondents. Results & Discussion: Correlation between knowledge of rural and urban women with age (r=0.235 & 0.281), caste (r=0.483 & 0.425), education (r=0.315 & 0.424), mass media utilization (r=0.410 & 0.394), Extension personnel contact (r=0.395 & 0.295) was positive and significant at 1 and 5 percent levels of significance whereas family type and annual income of rural and urban women were non-significantly correlated. Social participation of urban women with knowledge was also non-significantly correlated. Correlation between attitude of rural and urban women with age (r=0.222 & 0.293), caster (r=0.289 & 0.496), education (r=0.377 & 0.414), mass media utilization (r=0.340 & 0.310), Extension personnel contact (r=0.367 & 0.278) was positive and significant at 1 and 5 percent levels of significance whereas family type and annual income of rural and urban women were non-significantly correlated. Social participation of urban women with attitude was also non-significantly correlated. The findings of the data reveals the fact that there was a positive significant relationship between age, caste, education, family size, mass media exposure, and extension personal contact with knowledge and attitude about women empowerment schemes. Significance: The findings of this study have vast practical utility. This study would be useful for the stakeholders, policy makers, governmental and non- governmental agencies, cooperatives, and other inventories which are working for the development of women. Ministry of rural development, Government of India has taken initiatives for empowerment of women to all the rural poor families i.e. BPL and available decent quality of life. Various women empowerment schemes have initiatives which emerges as an important strategy for empowering women by providing loan subsidy to members of SHG and also enables livelihood opportunities for village women through microcredit with existing banks in the area..

ANALYSIS OF IMPROVED TOMATO HYBRIDS CULTIVATED AND SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURAL PRACTICES IN SOUTHWEST, NIGERIA
venue: International Journal of Agriculture Environment and Bioresearch
abstract: The study investigated the improved tomato hybrids cultivated and sustainable agricultural practices in southwest Nigeria. Specifically, the study aimed to examine the socio-economic characteristics of tomato farmers, describe the main improved varieties available and cultivated by the farmers; examine the SAP adopted by the farmers and determine factors affecting the varieties cultivated and number of SAP adopted by the farmers. The first stage involved deliberate selection of Osun and Ekiti States due to their large populations of tomato producers while the second phase also required the intentional selection of three (3) LGAs from each state according to the density of tomato farmers. A total of thirty (30) villages were included in the study by purposefully selecting five (5) villages from each LGA identified in the second phase. In the final phase, three hundred (300) tomato farmers were surveyed, which involved randomly selecting ten (10) farmers from each village. Descriptive statistics and Poisson regression analysis were used to analyze the data. The study discovered that among the numerous tomato hybrids available in southwest Nigeria, fourteen varieties were identified, with Platinum F1 being the most preferred at 24.2%, followed closely was Padma F1 at 22.3%, both of which are from the same brand (East West Seed International). The perceptions of the respondents regarding the characteristics of improved tomato varieties were assessed and the results revealed that tomato size (9.7%) is the primary attribute valued by the farmers in the study area. The findings from the statements about sustainable practices, categorized under ten (10) SAP indicators, indicated that Soil Health (% Mean = 26.0), Soil Loss (% Mean = 31.8), Integrated Pest Management (% Mean = 37.8), and Biodiversity (% Mean = 25.5) were adopted to some extent, while the Value of the Product (% Mean=61.2), Social and Human Capital (% Mean = 70.0) , and Local Economy(% Mean = 55.7) were fully embraced by the participants in the study area. There was minimal to no adoption concerning Nutrients (% Mean = 0.3), Energy (% Mean = 3.6), and Water Conservation (% Mean = 7.5). The results of the Poisson Regression model showed that education (p < 0.10), farm labourers (p < 0.05), income status (p < 0.05), access to credit (p < 0.05) and planting time (p < 0.05) were statistically significant and had a positive correlation to the number of improved tomato hybrids cultivated revealing a unit increase in these factors will increase the likelihood of cultivating more improved hybrids in the study area. Similarly, out of the fourteen variables analysed as factors that influence the number of SAP adopted, soil quality, tenancy status, gender and access to extension agents had a negative relationship with the number of SAP adopted, meaning they were less likely to have an impact on the number of SAP adopted in the study area. In contrast, factors like farmers' education, family size, access to credit, period of planting, and farm size which were significant at 5% probability level cum farm workers and income status (P < 0.01), had a positive correlation with the number of SAP adopted, suggesting that an increase of one unit of these factors would likely affect the number of SAP adopted in the study area.
